40 minutes from Nafplio. The famous ancient theatre.
A horseshoe of white marble seats, rebuilt for the first modern Olympics in 1896 on the site of an ancient stadium.
It’s the only stadium in the world built entirely of marble. Locals call it Kallimarmaro, “beautiful marble”.
The opening ceremony of the first modern Olympics was held here in 1896.
The Olympic flame is handed over here to each new host country, and the Athens Marathon finishes here every year.
A shady park behind Parliament with a duck pond and café, opening at its south end onto the neoclassical Zappeion Hall.
Queen Amalia commissioned the garden in 1838. Her gardener brought in more than 500 plant species, plus peacocks, ducks and turtles.
The Zappeion was the first building put up specifically for the revival of the Olympic Games, and it hosted fencing in 1896.
Greece signed its treaty to join the European Communities inside the Zappeion in 1979.
Athens’ central square, in front of the Parliament building, which was once the royal palace. The Evzones guard the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier below it.
Syntagma means “Constitution”. An uprising on 3 September 1843 forced King Otto to grant one, and the square was renamed after it.
The guard changes every hour on the hour. On Sundays at 11:00 there’s a big ceremony with a band.
Each guard’s clog (tsarouchi) weighs about 3 kg, with at least 60 nails in the sole. The story that the kilt has 400 pleats, one for each year of Ottoman rule, is probably a legend.
A glass museum at the foot of the hill, opened in 2009, holding the original sculptures from the Acropolis.
Glass floors let you look down into an excavated ancient Athenian neighbourhood under the building.
The top floor is turned to match the Parthenon’s exact orientation, and the frieze is shown in the order it once ran around the temple.
Five of the six original Caryatids stand here. The sixth’s spot is left empty, waiting for her return from the British Museum.
Huge Corinthian columns, all that’s left of what was once the largest temple in Greece, next to Hadrian’s Arch.
It took about 638 years to finish: work began in the 6th century BC and Emperor Hadrian dedicated it in AD 132.
